content:
Currently we have the Hilbert space for single-particle QM on Space d defined as a specific instance of an L2 space:

abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpace (d : ℕ) := Lp (α := Space d) ℂ 2 volume

I've been thinking about how best to generalize this to L2(Ω,C)L^2(\Omega, \mathbb{C})L2(Ω,C) for Ω\OmegaΩ a subset of Space d for use with the infinite square well, for example.
As I see it, there are at least 4 options:

abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpace_1 (d : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Space d) := volume) := Lp ℂ 2 μ
abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpace_2 (d : ℕ) (Ω : Set (Space d) := univ) := Lp (α := Ω) ℂ 2 volume
abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpace_3 (d : ℕ) (Ω : Set (Space d) := univ) := Lp ℂ 2 (volume.restrict Ω)
abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpace_4 (d : ℕ) (Ω : Set (Space d) := univ) : ClosedSubmodule ℂ (SpaceDHilbertSpace d) where
    carrier := {ψ ∈ SpaceDHilbertSpace d | ψ =ᵐ[volume.restrict Ωᶜ] 0}  -- or something equivalent
    ...
  1. Option 1 is the most flexible, allowing for one to consider, for example, the s-wave sector of some d-dimensional quantum system as a 1d system with non-standard measure or domains such as a spherical shell which have measure zero (options 2-4 are trivial when volume Ω = 0). For subsets with non-zero volume one could then use SpaceDHilbertSpace_1 d (volume.restrict Ω) as a special case.
  2. Option 2 seems like a poor choice since we lose all of the nice structure held by Space d and we lose Schwartz maps: 𝓢(Ω, ℂ) requires NormedAddCommGroup Ω.
  3. Option 3 I think would be the clear choice if not for the annoying fact that for the Hilbert space on all of Space d, presumably the most common case, the measure is volume.restrict univ and this is not definitionally equal to volume. A good API would ameliorate this.
  4. Option 4 makes mapping between various sub-Hilbert spaces easy, but requires a separate definition for SpaceDHilbertSpace d. It also has a more restrictive notion of Schwartz submodule: (SpaceDHilbertSpace_4 d Ω) ⊓ (SchwartzSubmodule d) consists of Schwartz maps which not only have domain a subset of Ω but all derivatives must vanish on the boundary of Ω.

I'm curious what others think about these options, or if there is an option I haven't considered.

Option 3 is a specialization of option 1, so I think we would favor option 1 over option 3. I think Option 2 is a no-go for the reason you said.

Option 4, I'm not sure if it actually captures what we need, would it for example even capture the eigenfunctions of the infinite well?

One thing I like about Option 1 is that it makes it absolutely clear why you actually need almost everywhere equal equivalence classes of square integrable functions, since 'almost everywhere' is governed by μ - so you don't care what happens outside the infinite well.

(4) does capture the infinite well eigenfunction but as the equivalence class of a piecewise function which is sine inside the well and zero outside. In contrast for (3) and by extension (1) the eigenfunction is just the equivalence class of sin⁡(nπx)\sin(n\pi x)sin(nπx) since the values outside the well don't matter.

Okay, thanks I will go ahead with (1). Perhaps something like

abbrev SpaceDHilbertSpaceOn {d :  ℕ) (Ω : Set (Space d)) := SpaceDHilbertSpace d (volume.restrict Ω)

will prove useful in the future.

I think you're talking about two similar but distinct operations here and we probably want some form of both (1) and (3). In a mathematical sense changing the measure is changing the Hilbert space and you can do that even without changing the underlying set. Restricting a measure to a subset is more like restricting to a subspace since you have a compatibility with the measure on the larger space. Perhaps the distinction is not physically important but I think it answers the formalization question.

I think you want to use (1) to generalize the standard Hilbert space to one where you can choose the measure, and therefore get a whole collection of Hilbert spaces on the same underlying set. Separately, there is a general construction to take any Hilbert space (including the specific one we're talking about here) and restrict to a subset by restricting the measure. You end up with two ways of writing the same thing but they're isomorphic and can map between them. This would be similar to the distinction in Mathlib between Group G and Subgroup G- the first being an instance and the second being a type that inherits the instance. You have the same sort of "duplication" effect where the group is isomorphic to the subgroup with carrier the full set. Then you develop API to make moving between the full space and the subspace easier.

Make sense!
SpaceDHilbertSpace d (μ.restrict Ω) being (isomorphic to) a subspace of SpaceDHilbertSpace d μ is clear to me, but more generally MemHS f μ implies MemHS f μ' whenever μ' ≤ μ; is there a good way to think of SpaceDHilbertSpace d μ' as a subspace of SpaceDHilbertSpace d μ when the measures are related in this way?
Thinking about things a bit more, I'm slightly worried that SpaceDHilbertSpace_1 does not force the wavefunctions to be zero at the edge of the infinite-well, if I am not mistaken?
(Sorry never mind, seems like the Hilbert space does not encode this information in general)

@Gregory Loges I think docs#MeasureTheory.Lp.LpToLpOfMeasureLeSMul is sort of what you're looking for. However I'd imagine this is unlikely to be injective since mu' a.e. equal may not imply mu a.e. equal. So you can map between the spaces but there isn't this nice correspondence. This is essentially what I meant by these operations being slightly different. Restricting to a subset creates a subspace since the restricted measure maintains a lot of the info of the original measure but changing the measure fundamentally changes the Hilbert space and the compatibility isn't as nice even when the measures are related.

This is very much not my area of expertise so I could be wrong, take my thoughts with a grain of salt, but I think this is at least approximately right. :blush:

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Yes, just to be clear this info shows up in the definition of the hamiltonian operator's domain to ensure it is symmetric (IBP terms vanish).

Okay, great that matches my expectation. Thanks for pointing me in the right direction in the docs.

physlib#1380 gets the basics in place and next I'll aim to define (subspaceIncl Ω).range as a submodule of SpaceDHilbertSpace d μ and make sure we have all of the various equivalences/(star)projections between the related spaces.
